claims.text: The starting alloy is equiatomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW.
NbMoTaW retains outstanding mechanical performance up to 1600 °C.
Equiatomic NbMoTaW has poor room-temperature ductility.
The irradiation resistance of NbMoTaW has only been inferred computationally.
Adding approximately 5 at% Ti and applying thermo-mechanical processing will enable controlled precipitate formation in NbMoTaW.
Ti-modified NbMoTaW will have a room-temperature duplex microstructure consisting of a continuous disordered BCC matrix and coherent nanoscale precipitates.
Ti-induced local lattice distortion will favor nucleation of fine precipitates during solidification and heat treatment.
The precipitates will disrupt crack propagation.
The precipitates will enhance dislocation mobility and thereby improve room-temperature ductility.
Precipitate–matrix interfaces will act as recombination centers for irradiation-induced point defects.
Above approximately 800 °C, the precipitates will coarsen or dissolve and the alloy will revert to a homogeneous BCC phase.
The Ti-modified alloy will preserve the high-temperature BCC phase stability of undoped NbMoTaW.
The Ti-modified alloy will preserve the high-temperature strength of undoped NbMoTaW.
The Ti-modified alloy will exhibit more than a 20% improvement in room-temperature fracture strain relative to undoped NbMoTaW.
The Ti-modified alloy will have a lower post-irradiation defect density than undoped NbMoTaW.
The Ti-modified alloy will exhibit less irradiation-induced blistering than undoped NbMoTaW.
The proposed irradiation benefit applies at room temperature under moderate helium-ion doses.
Excessive alloying or excessive secondary-phase formation can compromise the intended balance of properties.

contradictions.description: Precipitate dissolution could produce a homogeneous phase, but precipitate coarsening ordinarily retains a distinct precipitate phase; therefore, the assertion that either coarsening or dissolution restores homogeneous single-phase BCC is internally inconsistent.

The predicted outcome requires preservation of high-temperature performance, which permits performance to remain unchanged relative to the baseline, whereas the falsification rule lists unchanged high-temperature performance as part of a falsifying result.
